_about: HFACS levels and Nanocode prefixes as they appear in ProbeMatrix exports. A Nanocode such as 'OIR 1.1' is a prefix ('OIR') plus a factor number; the prefix fixes the level and the sub-category. 'subcategory' is the export's own Subcategory string, character for character (note the spaces after '/'), so it can be matched against findings.json. 'plain' is a one-line plain-language reading for non-specialist audiences. Every prefix here was seen in the public Hazira sample export. Classic HFACS categories that ProbeMatrix may also emit are listed in hfacs-levels.md, not here, until their prefixes are confirmed; add them with "seen_in_sample": false. Human-readable companion: hfacs-levels.md.

1.name: Unsafe Acts
1.definition: What people at the sharp end did or did not do in the moments before the event: errors (judgement and decision, skill-based, perception) and violations (departures from a rule or procedure). A level 1 finding describes an act, never the person's character.

2.name: Preconditions
2.definition: The conditions in place at the time of the act that made it more likely: the physical, technological and task environment, the state of the people involved (perception, fatigue, attention) and how the team coordinated, communicated and planned.

3.name: Supervision
3.definition: How work was planned, resourced, checked and corrected by first-line and middle supervision: oversight that was not enough, operations planned in a way that carried risk, known problems left uncorrected, and supervisory departures from rules.

4.name: Organisational Influences
4.definition: The decisions, systems and norms set by the organisation that shape every level below: resources (people, money, equipment), policies and processes, organisational climate and culture, and how people are selected and staffed.

AJDE.plain: A choice made with the information and time available turned out to be the wrong one, for example continuing a task when the plan no longer fitted the situation.

APE.plain: What a person saw, heard or sensed did not match what was really there, for example misreading a gauge in poor light.

ASBE.plain: A practised, routine action went wrong in its execution, for example a step skipped or done out of order during a familiar job.

AV.plain: Work departed from a rule or procedure, often because the departure had become the normal way of working; the learning is about why the rule did not fit the work.

PPE.plain: The physical surroundings made the work harder or riskier, for example heat, noise, darkness, weather or a congested layout.

PPI.subcategory: Condition of Individuals - Perceptual Factors/ Sensory Misperception
PPI.plain: The conditions of the task made it hard for people to perceive the hazard correctly, for example a gas release that could not be seen or smelt.

PSE.plain: The way the task or situation was set up added risk, for example time pressure, simultaneous operations or an unusual plant state.

PTE.plain: Equipment, instruments, controls or design did not support safe work, for example a detector that was out of service or a display that hid an alarm.

PTF.subcategory: Personnel Factors - Teamwork (Coordination/ Communication/ Planning Factors)
PTF.plain: Information, coordination or planning between people and teams did not work, for example a handover that left out a live hazard.

SVF.plain: A problem was already known to supervision, through reports, defects or audits, and was not put right before the event.

SVI.plain: Oversight, guidance or checking of the work was not enough for the risk, for example no one confirming that isolations were in place.

SVIO.plain: The work was planned or scheduled in a way that carried more risk than it should, for example running a job with too few people or out of sequence.

SVV.plain: Supervision knowingly allowed or directed work outside the rules, for example authorising a task without the required permit.

OIC.plain: The shared norms, priorities and signals from leadership shaped how work was really done, for example production being valued above reporting concerns.

OIP.plain: Company policies, procedures or management processes were missing, unclear or did not fit the work, for example no process to review a known design weakness.

OIR.plain: The organisation did not provide the people, money, equipment or time the work needed, for example deferring a replacement because of budget.

OIS.plain: How people were selected, placed and staffed left gaps in competence or numbers, for example a role filled without the required qualification.
